title: Scaling Ray for AI workloads to 10k node clusters | Anyscale
gist: Anyscale details a year of Ray Core rework that took placement-group readiness from hours to seconds (62x faster at 2,000 nodes, 303x at 10,000), made batch inference 23% and shuffle 24% faster, and now supports 40,000 actors on 10,000-node clusters — driven by RL and pre-/post-training users running 2,000-10,000 node topology-constrained clusters where idle GPU time at launch and after every failure is the binding cost.

themes.theme: Demand signal: frontier training pushes Ray to 10k nodes

insights.claim: Ray users are now running large-scale RL and pre-/post-training on clusters of 2,000 to 10,000 nodes with tens of thousands of actors under network topology constraints, making cluster startup and failure-restart time the critical metric.
insights.speaker: Yicheng Lu
insights.so_what: Confirms frontier-scale RL/post-training is a mainstream open-source workload, not just hyperscaler-internal — a tailwind for AI-infra orchestration vendors and GPU cluster demand.
insights.quote: These run on clusters from 2,000 to 10,000 nodes, with tens of thousands of actors scheduled under network topology constraints.
insights.locator: As Ray is used in more and more emerging

insights.claim: Because an NCCL communicator is all-or-nothing, one dead node forces every actor in a training run to restart, so users pay the idle-GPU cost of full cluster relaunch at every single failure, not just at initial launch.
insights.speaker: Yicheng Lu
insights.so_what: Failure-recovery speed compounds with cluster size and failure rates — a structural moat for whoever solves fast restart; also quantifies why reliability tooling is monetizable at GPU-hour prices.
insights.quote: an NCCL communicator is all-or-nothing and one dead node means restarting every actor
insights.locator: Apart from the above Ray Data workloads

insights.claim: A canonical topology-aware training setup on NVIDIA GB200/GB300 NVL72 racks maps one Ray placement group per 18-node rack with 4 actors per node — 18x4 matching the 72 GPUs in NVL72 — showing rack-scale NVLink domains are now the scheduling unit for training software.
insights.speaker: Yicheng Lu
insights.so_what: Software stacks are being rebuilt around NVIDIA's rack-scale NVL72 topology — evidence the GB200/GB300 rack architecture is becoming the standard deployment unit, reinforcing NVIDIA's systems-level lock-in.
insights.quote: one placement group per rack of 18 nodes, one bundle per node, 4 actors inside each bundle, each corresponding to one GPU in the rack, 18 times 4 being exactly the 72 in NVL72
insights.locator: They also care about network topology constraints

insights.claim: Engineers from Google and ByteDance are credited contributors to Ray's 10,000-node scaling effort, indicating hyperscalers and top AI labs are co-investing in Ray as shared training infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Yicheng Lu
insights.so_what: Ray's ecosystem gravity across US and Chinese hyperscalers strengthens Anyscale's strategic position and Ray's status as default AI-compute substrate.
insights.locator: We'd like to thank the following people

insights.claim: One year of Ray Core work delivered 23% faster end-to-end batch inference on 500 nodes, 24% faster Ray Data shuffle, 62x faster placement-group readiness at 2,000 nodes, 303x faster at 10,000 nodes, and 6.5x faster end-to-end actor launch at 2,000 nodes.
insights.speaker: Yicheng Lu
insights.so_what: Orders-of-magnitude launch-time gains directly cut idle-GPU burn for training customers — watch for Anyscale converting this into enterprise wins versus Kubernetes-native and proprietary schedulers.
insights.quote: 62× faster to get placement groups ready at 2,000 nodes.303× faster to get placement groups ready at 10,000 nodes.
insights.locator: After a round of Ray Core improvements

insights.claim: Ray can now run 40,000 actors on a 10,000-node cluster, a scale it could not support a year earlier, and all the fixes are already shipped in Ray nightly.
insights.speaker: Yicheng Lu
insights.so_what: The 10k-node ceiling is a competitive benchmark against Slurm/Kubernetes for frontier training; capability is shipping now, not roadmap vapor.
insights.quote: Scales to 40,000 actors on a 10,000 node cluster, a scale it could not support a year ago.
insights.locator: After a round of Ray Core improvements

themes.theme: A reusable taxonomy of distributed-systems bottlenecks

insights.claim: Across both data pipelines and 10,000-node training clusters, Ray's scaling bottlenecks reduced to just three recurring patterns: lock contention between threads, a single overwhelmed async thread, and scheduling on stale resource views.
insights.speaker: Yicheng Lu
insights.so_what: A diligence lens for any distributed AI-infra stack: ask vendors how they handle these three failure modes; systems that haven't hit them likely haven't been run at scale.
insights.quote: Lock contention between threads.A single overwhelmed thread handling async work.Scheduling on stale resource views.
insights.locator: The bottlenecks we found kept falling

insights.claim: On a 500-node batch inference workload, a single publish lock contended by Ray's Python and C threads consumed 17.4% of the scheduling loop's time; moving all publishing onto one thread eliminated the contention entirely.
insights.speaker: Yicheng Lu
insights.so_what: Double-digit performance was hiding in one lock — evidence that AI-infra efficiency gains (and cost curves) still have substantial low-hanging software headroom before new hardware is needed.
insights.quote: the publish lock alone was eating 17.4% of the scheduling loop's time

insights.claim: In one Ray shuffle run, over a million tiny argument-check callbacks occupied about 17% of the background thread's time — each taking 0.04 ms to run after waiting 5.7 seconds in queue — and skipping checks for already-produced arguments alone made shuffles 9.2% faster end to end.
insights.speaker: Yicheng Lu
insights.so_what: Queue delay, not compute, was the tax: a 140,000x wait-to-work ratio per callback shows why single-threaded control planes cap AI pipeline throughput.
insights.quote: each one taking 0.04 ms to run after waiting 5.7 seconds for its turn
insights.locator: The first problem we found was a flood

insights.claim: Skipping location subscriptions for objects already on the local node cut Ray's driver publishing traffic in half, and the combined driver fixes lifted sustained task throughput by up to 1.6x.
insights.speaker: Yicheng Lu
insights.so_what: Data-locality-aware pruning of control traffic is a generalizable pattern; 1.6x throughput on the same hardware is a direct inference-cost deflator.
insights.locator: The second problem jumped straight out

insights.claim: Ray's global control service (GCS) was made multithreaded and its load lightened, cutting idle main-thread utilization on a zero-job 10,000-node cluster from about 61% on Ray 2.51 to about 38% on the current nightly.
insights.speaker: Yicheng Lu
insights.so_what: A control plane that was 61% consumed before any work arrived was the hidden ceiling on cluster size — headroom recovered here is what unlocks the 10k-node tier.
insights.quote: a 10,000 node cluster with zero jobs submitted already kept the GCS main thread about 61% busy; on today's nightly, the same idle cluster sits at about 38%
insights.locator: Keeping the GCS Stable at 10,000 Nodes

insights.claim: A defensive three-second resource-view reset, designed to fix leaked optimistic deductions, backfired at scale: it made filled nodes look empty faster than the slow syncer could correct them, so the scheduler kept sending placement groups to already-full nodes — removing the reset for the GCS collapsed 10,000-node placement-group scheduling from hours to seconds.
insights.speaker: Yicheng Lu
insights.so_what: A safety mechanism became the bottleneck at scale — a recurring pattern worth probing in any infra diligence; the fix was deletion, not addition.
insights.quote: the insurance itself became the problem
insights.locator: Placement Groups: From Hours to Seconds

insights.claim: Ray's pg.ready() API secretly submitted a dummy task that inherited the job's runtime environment, so a simple readiness check could block on a torch install, and the common user loop of ray.get(pg.ready()) serialized a thousand placement groups into a thousand sequential round trips; it is now a direct async GCS query with the task removed.
insights.speaker: Yicheng Lu
insights.so_what: API sugar with hidden mechanics becomes a scaling tax; latency users blamed on cluster size was an implementation artifact now removed.
insights.quote: a simple resource check could sit waiting for a torch install to finish
insights.locator: The other part of the slowness

insights.claim: At 10,000 nodes Ray's resource-view syncer took around 200 seconds to propagate at peak, leaving the head node scheduling actors on views minutes behind reality and triggering cascading reject-and-reschedule storms as the cluster filled.
insights.speaker: Yicheng Lu
insights.so_what: Gossip-style state fan-out to N nodes breaks at frontier scale — expect all schedulers at this tier to converge on centralized or hierarchical designs.
insights.quote: At the 10,000 node level we have seen it take around 200 seconds to propagate at peak.
insights.locator: The first problem is that the syncer

insights.claim: Anyscale is walking back Ray's founding assumption that every node can schedule, moving toward centralized scheduling where only a few nodes hold the full cluster resource view, and is moving non-detached actor lifecycle management out of the GCS to the owner to eliminate the per-actor multi-message conversation that currently replays en masse on every restart.
insights.speaker: Yicheng Lu
insights.so_what: A rare public reversal of a core architectural bet; if it lands, actor restart cost drops sharply — watch Ray release notes as the leading indicator of the next step-change in training-cluster efficiency.
insights.quote: we are walking back the assumption this whole design started from, that every node can schedule
insights.locator: To solve the problem, we are currently working

insights.claim: Restart amplification is structural in Ray today: because every actor holds a standing subscription on the GCS, a single node failure in a training run makes tens of thousands of subscriptions fire back at the GCS simultaneously while the full registration conversation replays once per actor.
insights.speaker: Yicheng Lu
insights.so_what: Failure events create thundering-herd load exactly when the control plane is most stressed — quantifies the reliability risk embedded in large synchronous training runs.
insights.quote: Tens of thousands of standing subscriptions fire back at the GCS at the same moment
